summary:
Tasmania's Anti-Discrimination Act 1998 prohibits discrimination on the grounds of gender identity, gender expression, sex characteristics and variations of sex characteristics. A September 2013 amendment extended the Act's reach to transgender and intersex people and made it unlawful to offend, humiliate, intimidate, insult or ridicule a person on the basis of actual or perceived gender, sexual orientation or gender identity. The 2019 amendments to the same Act added gender expression, gender identity expressly defined to include being transgender or transsexual and identifying or living as another gender, and sex characteristics and variations of sex characteristics, including as grounds for the prohibition on incitement to hatred.

Legal gender recognition operates on a self-declaration basis. The Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration Amendment Act 2019 received royal assent on 8 May 2019 and took effect on 5 September 2019, and no medical certificate or other medical document is required. A person aged 16 or over may register male, female, indeterminate gender, non-binary, or another self-described gender that is neither entirely male nor female, by statutory declaration of identity and of the gender lived or sought to be lived; the Registrar may refuse a term outside the prescribed list. The same reforms removed any requirement to undergo surgery or divorce, made the gender entry on a birth certificate optional so that a descriptor can be removed entirely, allowed parents or guardians to register a gender for children under 16 supported by the child's own declaration where the child is able to give it, and extended the registration period for parents of intersex children to 120 days after birth. Birth sex registration remains male-or-female only and cannot be changed except to correct an initial error, but it ceases once a gender registration is made. Tasmania issues 'X' sex descriptors on birth certificates as of 2019.

The 2019 birth-certificate reforms passed the House of Assembly on 10 April 2019 after the Liberal Speaker crossed the floor to vote with the Opposition, the bill having already passed the Legislative Council. The Tasmanian Government opposed the amendments and declined to rule out a later repeal.

The age of consent in Tasmania is 17 years, equal for all forms of sexual activity; only South Australia shares that figure. Tasmania was the final Australian jurisdiction to decriminalise male homosexuality, with effect from 14 May 1997.

A hate crimes bill passed the lower house in September 2025 and would explicitly include gender identity within the 1997 sentencing act; the upper house had not voted on it as at the date of that reporting. As of September 2026, conversion therapy practices remain legally permitted in Tasmania.

No state-specific incident series or enforcement pattern for gender-identity offences is documented in the sources reviewed, and no charging or prosecution data for the proposed sentencing provisions appears.
tangentialFactors:
Tasmania's cross-dressing offence under section 8(1)(d) of the Police Offences Act 1935 was repealed on 12 April 2001, and Tasmania is described as the only Australian state to have criminalised cross-dressing at all. The offence carried penalties for the wearing of disguise by a man in a public place, and its repeal predates the gender-recognition reforms by eighteen years.

Consensual homosexual activity was decriminalised by the Criminal Code Amendment Act 1997, passed 1 May 1997, receiving assent 13 May 1997 and taking effect the following day, after penalties of up to 21 years that were described as the harshest in the Western world. The change followed the United Nations Human Rights Committee decision in Toonen on 31 March 1994 and the federal Human Rights (Sexual Conduct) Act 1994, which legalised adult consensual sexual activity in private nationally; Tasmania still refused to repeal its Criminal Code provisions and acted only when faced with a likely High Court loss in Croome v Tasmania.

Same-sex couples in Tasmania can enter registered domestic partnerships with an optional official ceremony, and equality of adoption rights for same-sex couples applied across all states and territories from April 2018.
localsOnly:
Charges and convictions for cross-dressing offences under the Police Offences Act 1935 as in force before 12 April 2001, including attempts and inciting, instigating, aiding or abetting, are eligible for expungement on application to the Secretary under the Expungement of Historical Offences Act 2017, which received royal assent on 21 November 2017. Applications may be made by the charged person or, where that person is deceased or lacks capacity, by specified representatives. Historic convictions for consensual homosexual activity before 1997 are eligible for expungement from 9 April 2018 under the same Act, following a parliamentary apology on 13 April 2017, and compensation of up to $75,000 becomes available from 2 August 2026.

Parents and guardians of a Tasmanian-registered child under 16 may register a gender for that child, supported by the child's own gender declaration where the child is able to give it, or otherwise by statements of consistency with the child's will and preference together with optional counselling evidence for a child under 18.

Registered domestic partnerships are available to same-sex couples with an optional ceremony, and de facto partners nationally face longer eligibility periods and a heavier burden of proof than married couples when dealing with government departments.
outOfScopeNotes:
The hate crimes bill that passed the Tasmanian lower house in September 2025 had not been voted on by the upper house at the time of the reporting available here; whether it has since been enacted, amended or lapsed is unresolved in these sources.

The Tasmanian Government's stated position in April 2019 was opposition to the birth-certificate reforms, and it declined to rule out a later repeal. Whether any repeal was subsequently attempted or carried out is unresolved in these sources.

No Tasmania-specific data on access to gender-affirming health care, waiting times, facility access or hospital policy appears in the inventory; those questions are not sourced at this level.

No charging, prosecution or sentencing data exists in these sources for gender-identity provisions of the Anti-Discrimination Act 1998 or for the proposed sentencing amendment, so enforcement of the protections is not evidenced either way.

Whether conversion therapy is practised in Tasmania, and how often, is not sourced; the inventory establishes only that it remained legally permitted as of September 2026.
